lesson.title: What Ten Points Per Hour Actually Means
lesson.summary: The slope of a regression line is a rate, the predicted change in the response variable for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable, and stating it correctly requires naming both variables and their units.
lesson.body:
Every regression equation involves two roles for the variables, and naming them correctly is the first step toward interpreting the slope correctly. The explanatory variable is the one used to predict or account for changes in the other, and it is placed on the horizontal axis. The response variable is the outcome being predicted, and it is placed on the vertical axis. In the running example, hours studied is the explanatory variable and exam score is the response variable, since it makes practical sense to use study time to predict a score, not the other way around.

The slope of a regression equation is a rate of change, and there is a consistent template for stating it in words: for each additional one unit of the explanatory variable, the predicted response variable changes by b1 units, on average. That phrase on average, or equivalently predicted, is not decoration, and it should never be dropped. The regression line is a summary of a trend across many individuals, not a guarantee about any single one of them, so a correct interpretation must reflect that it describes an expected change across the whole group, not a certain outcome for one person.

Applying the template to the worked example: b1 equals 10, so for each additional hour studied, predicted exam score increases by 10 points, on average. Every piece of that sentence is required for full credit and full clarity: the number 10, the unit of x, hours studied, the unit of y, points, the direction, increases, and the qualifier, on average. Dropping any one of those pieces turns a correct, specific statistical statement into a vague or even misleading one.

The sign of the slope also reports the direction of the underlying association directly, echoing what was first seen on the scatterplot. A positive slope, as in this example, means the predicted response rises as the explanatory variable rises, matching the positive direction already identified visually. A negative slope would mean the predicted response falls as the explanatory variable rises, and a slope near zero would suggest little to no linear relationship at all, consistent with a correlation coefficient near zero for the same data.

This shared sign between slope and correlation is not a coincidence, it is guaranteed by the formula connecting them. Since the slope equals r times the ratio of the standard deviation of y to the standard deviation of x, and a standard deviation can never be negative, the sign of b1 is always exactly the sign of r itself. A positive correlation guarantees a positive slope, and a negative correlation guarantees a negative slope, so the direction of a relationship only ever needs to be determined once, whether it is read from the scatterplot, from r, or from the regression equation, all three will always agree.

A frequent error worth flagging directly: describing a slope as simply the increase in the score, without ever naming the unit of x it corresponds to. Ten points means nothing at all on its own, but ten points per additional hour studied, on average, is a complete, checkable statistical claim that someone else could verify.
